'''''Oxalis violacea''''', the '''violet wood-sorrel''', is a [[perennial plant]] and [[herb]] in the family [[Oxalidaceae]].<ref name="grin">{{GRIN | accessdate = 21 January 2018}}</ref> It is native to the eastern and central United States.

==Description==
''Oxalis violacea'' emerges in early spring from an underground [[bulb]] and produces leaf stems {{cvt|7-13|cm|in|frac=4}} tall and flower [[umbels]], or clusters, with up to 19 flowers on stems {{cvt|9-23|cm|in|frac=4}} tall.<ref name="FNA">{{eFloras|1 |first=Guy L. |last=Nesom |volume=12}}</ref> The three-part leaves have heart-shaped leaflets. The plant is similar in appearance to small [[clover]]s such as the [[shamrock]].

The plant bears lavender to white flowers {{cvt|1-2|cm|in|frac=4}} wide with white to pale green centers above the foliage, during April or May,<!-- Any data on flower time in southern part of range? --> rarely to July, and, with rain, sometimes produces additional flowers without leaves from August to October.<ref name="FNA" />

==Etymology==
The genus name, Oxalis, is from the Greek word oxys, which means "sharp" and refers to the sharp or sour taste from the oxalic acid present in the plant.<ref>{{cite web |title=oxalis - WordReference.com Dictionary of English |url=https://www.wordreference.com/definition/oxalis |website=www.wordreference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Denison |first1=Edgar |title=Missouri Wildflowers |date=2017 |publisher=Conservation Commission of the State of Missouri |isbn=978-1-887247-59-7 |pages=58 |edition=Sixth}}</ref> The specific epithet, violacea, is Latin for violet-colored.<ref>{{cite web |title=Latin Definition for: violaceus, violacea, violaceum (ID: 38867) - Latin Dictionary and Grammar Resources - Latdict |url=https://latin-dictionary.net/definition/38867/violaceus-violacea-violaceum |website=latin-dictionary.net}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is [[native plant]] in much of the [[United States]], from the [[Rocky Mountains]] east to the Atlantic Ocean and [[Gulf of Mexico]] coasts, and through [[Eastern Canada]].  It has a tendency to cluster in open places in damp woods and on stream banks, and in moist [[prairie]]s.<ref name="grin"/>

==Conservation==
The plant's conservation status is globally secure;<ref>{{cite web |title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0 |url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Taxon/ELEMENT_GLOBAL.2.158359/Oxalis_violacea |website=explorer.natureserve.org}}</ref> however, it is listed as endangered in Massachusetts<ref>{{cite web |title=List of Endangered, Threatened, and Special Concern species {{!}} Mass.gov |url=https://www.mass.gov/info-details/list-of-endangered-threatened-and-special-concern-species#plants |website=www.mass.gov |language=en}}</ref> and Rhode Island,<ref>{{cite web |title=Oxalis violacea (violet wood sorrel): Go Botany |url=https://gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org/species/oxalis/violacea/ |website=gobotany.nativeplanttrust.org}}</ref> threatened in New York,<ref>{{cite web |title=Violet Wood Sorrel Guide - New York Natural Heritage Program |url=https://guides.nynhp.org/violet-wood-sorrel/#:~:text=In%20New%20York%20Oxalis%20violacea,York%20Natural%20Heritage%20Program%202007). |website=guides.nynhp.org}}</ref> and a species of special concern in Connecticut.<ref>{{cite web |title=Oxalis violacea |url=https://www.ct-botanical-society.org/plants/Plants/view/423 |website=www.ct-botanical-society.org}}</ref> It is presumed [[extirpated]] in Michigan.<ref>{{cite web |title=Oxalis violacea (Violet wood sorrel) - Michigan Natural Features Inventory |url=https://mnfi.anr.msu.edu/species/description/14490/Oxalis-violacea |website=mnfi.anr.msu.edu}}</ref>

==Uses==

===Medicinal===
''Oxalis violacea'' was used as a [[medicinal plant]] by  [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]], including the [[Cherokee people|Cherokee]] and [[Pawnee people|Pawnee]] peoples.<ref name=uom>{{cite web |title=BRIT - Native American Ethnobotany Database |url=http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=oxalis+violacea |website=naeb.brit.org}}</ref>

===Culinary===
All parts of the plant are edible – flowers, leaves, stems, and bulb. [[Oxalis]] is from the Greek word meaning sour, and this plant has a sour juice.  It is used in salads.  Moderate use of plant is advisable, as it should not be eaten in large quantities due to a high concentration of [[oxalic acid]], ("salt of lemons") which can be poisonous.<ref>{{cite book | first1=Berndt | last1=Berglund | first2=Clare E. | last2=Bolsby | title=The Edible Wild: A complete cookbook and guide to edible wild plants in Canada and North America| year=1971 | publisher=Burns & MacEachern Limited—Pagurian Press Limited.}}</ref>

It was a traditional food source of the Native American [[Apache people|Apache]], Cherokee, [[Omaha people|Omaha]], Pawnee, and [[Ponca people|Ponca]] peoples.<ref name="uom"/>

===Cultivation===
''Oxalis violacea'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]], for use as a flowering [[groundcover]] or [[perennial plant]] in traditional and [[native plant]] gardens, and for [[natural landscaping]] projects.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=l340 |work=Plant Finder |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, Kemper Center for Home Gardening |title=''Oxalis violacea''}}</ref> It spreads rapidly by runners and bulbs.<ref name="npin">{{NPIN|OXVI|Oxalis violacea}}</ref> In gardens the plant prefers partial shade and moisture.<ref name="npin"/>
